newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Afghan peace still remote despite Taleban offer.
newsitem.headline: Afghan peace still remote despite Taleban offer.

text.p: Afghanistan's Islamic Taleban militia has offered renewed talks with its foes, but there are few signs that peace is any closer, diplomats said on Tuesday.

"There is still a strong belief among the warring leaders that they can win militarily," said a U.N. diplomat involved in peace efforts. "Currently one side is in a better position and it is always difficult to negotiate when there is an imbalance."
U.N. special envoy to Afghanistan Norbert Holl has been searching for what he calls a "balance of frustration" to underpin serious peace talks since he began work in July.
So far, he has little to show for his bid to resolve a conflict that also defied his predecessor, Mahmoud Mestiri.
The mainly ethnic Pashtun Taleban took the Afghan capital last September 27 from ousted president Burhanuddin Rabbani's Tajik-led government.
The capture prompted an opposition alliance between former military commander Ahmad Shah Masood and his old rival, General Abdul Rashid Dostum, whose troops are ethnic Uzbeks.

Holl brought three Taleban and three opposition delegates together for three days of talks in Islamabad last week, hailing the result as "concrete and practical agreement on several key points", including agreement to meet again next month.
The next day Taleban fighters assaulted and captured the Soviet-built military airbase at Bagram, about 50 km (30 miles) north of Kabul, and the opposition-held town of Charikar.
"Obviously we are disappointed and concerned at the resumption of hostilities, especially after the working group had begun face-to-face meetings," the U.N. diplomat said.
"It's a setback for U.N. peace efforts, but we don't give up just because fighting has broken out. We hope the hostilities won't send a wrong signal to the Ashgabat meeting."

He was referring to a two-day international meeting of donors, U.N. agencies and relief groups due to begin in the Turkmenistan capital on Tuesday to discuss how to keep aid flowing to Afghanistan's impoverished and war-weary people.
A different signal came from Kabul on Monday when acting Information Minister Amir Khan Mutaqi said the Taleban were ready for conditional talks with the opposition.
He said Masood and Dostum must declare willingness to stop hostilities, exchange prisoners and hold peace talks, but he rejected their key demand for demilitarisation of Kabul.
"There is no problem in Kabul. It is peaceful and it is irrational to demilitarise it," Mutaqi said.

The Taleban offer has drawn no response so far from the opposition alliance, known as the Supreme Council for the Defence of Afghanistan. Nor have any of the feuding factions responded to an Iranian offer to host peace talks in Tehran.
In Ashgabat, Holl will argue that only a political solution can reverse a decline in assistance, without proposing a direct link between humanitarian aid and progress towards peace.
U.N. officials, frustrated by the intractable nature of Afghanistan's factional war, see better coordination between humanitarian and diplomatic efforts as one way forward.

"After all, both are aimed for stability, for peace, and sometimes the use of a carrot may be useful to promote peace," Yasushi Akashi, U.N. Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs, told Reuters in Islamabad on Monday.

"We are very much interested in synchronising assistance with peace negotiations," he added. "When Afghans see the fruits of peace through a better life, maybe they will become more eager to negotiate a ceasefire, demilitarisation and so on."
For the moment, there is no sign that the Taleban, under their reclusive leader Mullah Mohammed Omar, have dropped their aim to spread their purist Islamic rule across Afghanistan.
Nor are Masood and Dostum, however shaky their alliance, showing any readiness to cede control of the Tajik- and Uzbek-populated north to the Taleban without a fight.
Afghanistan's neighbours -- Iran, Pakistan and the former Soviet Central Asian republics -- deny they are meddling in its affairs, but all factions say their foes get outside help.
U.N. diplomats believe that only a concerted international effort can untangle the knot of regional rivalries and their links to Afghan groups caught up in internecine fighting.
"You can talk of carrots and sticks, but we don't have too many of either," said one U.N. official. "We could involve major countries more directly, but we are still working on this."
